author: Leanne Sanders
title: Banner message along Edmonton area highway ‘racist’ according to First Nations
content: The photo of a banner hung from a barbed wire fence along highway 779 northwest of Edmonton went viral after it was posted online over the Heritage Day long weekend. “The Indians have done nothing in 100 years and now they wanna tell us how to run Alberta,” the banner said. It alarmed Kara Burnstick from Alexander First Nation enough that she stopped to take a picture of it. She told APTN News that it feels like attitudes toward First Nations people are getting worse. “A hundred percent. I think that you can definitely sense it, and you can definitely feel it. Just when I’m out, doing grocery shopping or getting gas or something. It’s very unsettling,” said Burnstick said on her social media post. While Burnstick doesn’t know when the banner was placed on the fence, the date of her photo coincided with an “Alberta Independence Walk” and rally by the group Cruise to Alberta Independence in Spruce Grove, south of where the banner was reportedly located. The group has promoted a series of rallies in support of the province separating across Alberta in recent months, ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum. APTN reached out to the group for comment. In an email, “Al Bertan” with the group said they were unaware of the banner. “This is not our approach, so it is definitely not something we would do. author: Jon Thompson
title: From wildfire to sewage crisis: Neskantaga’s nightmare isn’t over
content:
Only five days after members of Neskantaga First Nation returned home from the wildfire evacuation, a new emergency has its members on their way out again.

Chief and council of the fly-in northwestern Ontario First Nation declared a state of emergency on Tuesday, after sewage backed up and filled the basement of its beleaguered health centre.

Neskantaga Chief Gary Quisess said he’s disappointed the federal contractor who was working in the facility didn’t accept the offer of their local sewage pumping truck before doing the work that has now caused the second evacuation of the summer.

“It’s very disappointing. The community is really feeling it,” Quisess said.

“There’s going to be a lot of remediation. They’ve got to take the whole foundation out. The raw sewage doesn’t go anywhere when it seeps underground. It stays there until you remove it.”

The evacuation comes as the community of 350 people located 450 kilometres northeast of Thunder Bay returns from two weeks in Toronto hotels where they fled from the worst forest fire season in Ontario history.

It also comes as Neskantaga prepares for its week-long summer festival. The event, which welcomes off-reserve members home for feasts, games, and a pow wow, is cancelled.It’s the second time in as many years that the chief and council have ordered the health centre condemned. author: The Canadian Press
title: ‘Devastation’: Chief says about 230 homes destroyed by B.C. wildfire
content:
The chief of the Okanagan Indian Band says about 230 homes have been destroyed by a raging wildfire near Vernon, B.C., in one of the worst wildfire losses in recent Canadian history.

Dan Wilson said 30 homes of band members and 200 non-band homes had burned in the Bradley Creek fire, which evacuees said was fanned by powerful winds over the weekend.

Wilson said during a news conference on Tuesday that the reserve “looked like a war zone” when he took a helicopter tour of the area, at the northern end of Okanagan Lake in the B.C. Interior.

“It was hard to recognize my community from the air with all the structures and the forest gone.”

The wildfire has been one of the most devastating events in the band’s history, he said.

Wilson described the event as “surreal,” saying the scope of destruction was just sinking in.

The fire started late Friday and was fanned by winds gusting up to 115 kilometres per hour.

“The point that I really want to make to everyone is that the fire spread so fast that some of our members only had five minutes to evacuate,” Wilson said.

Wilson said his flyover showed just how close the nation came to losing key infrastructure, like the powwow arbour, a daycare centre and the new school, all of which were saved by aircraft saturating the area with water.

author: Leanne Sanders
title: RCMP say ‘reasonable force’ used in arrest of woman at Makwa Sagaiehcan First Nation on Monday
content:
Family and supporters of a Makwa Sahgaiehcan First Nation woman arrested on the weekend are staging two days of peaceful protest at the Loon Lake RCMP detachment in northern Saskatchewan. The arrest, captured by her daughter on cell phone video and shared to social media, has since gone viral with more than 2.7 million views.




“Look what they did to my poor mom. My mom’s never had anything to do with the law ever!” Teyonah Angus posted alongside the video. “She has no existing criminal record whatsoever. How is this acceptable for them to do this to my MOTHER. My mom’s name is ROSE GEORGINA ANGUS. She’s a 40 year old Indigenous Cree woman a mother of four, she’s someone’s baby, she’s someone’s mother, she’s someone’s cousin/niece auntie, SHE’S SOMEONE. And they treated her like she was nothing.”




The video shows a woman being taken to the ground by two RCMP officers. One can be heard saying “when I say get the (expletive) back from me, you get back. Do you hear me? (Expletive) unacceptable.”




Once in handcuffs and on the ground, the officer goes on to demand the woman get up, even though she is handcuffed and on her stomach. When she is brought to her feet, she is visibly bloodied.




A taser can also be heard going off in the video.
